title: The General Solution is a Superposition of Normal Modes
lead: The spatial and temporal equations of a string held at both ends are solved one at a time, and the solutions they give are multiplied together and then added up.
objectives: Separate the wave equation into individual spatial and temporal problems and solve them.
Demonstrate that the general solution can be a superposition of solutions (normal modes)
notes: Adapted from Michael Fowler (University of Virginia) under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; Exercise 2.3.1, printed in Section 2.3, is set here because it adds two waves together.
exercise_notes: Exercises 2.3.1 and 2.4.1 and their keys are the book's; 2.3.1 is printed in Section 2.3 and set here because it tests superposition. The last two exercises, on the frequencies of normal modes and a sum of two modes, were written by AI with AI solutions. Bloom levels and concept tags were chosen by AI. Numeric answers accept a 2% tolerance.

exercises.prompt:
Given two traveling waves:

$$ \psi_1 = \sin{(c_1 x+c_2 t)} \; \textrm{ and } \; \psi_2 = \sin{(c_1 x-c_2 t)} $$
  1. Find the wavelength and the wave velocity of $\psi_1$ and $\psi_2$

  2. Find the following and identify nodes:

    $$ \psi_+ = \psi_1 + \psi_2 \; \textrm{ and } \; \psi_- = \psi_1 - \psi_2 $$

answer.solution:
Solution a

$\psi_1$ is a sin function. At every integer $n \pi$ where $n=0,\pm 1, \pm 2, ...$, a sin function will be zero. Thus, $\psi_1 = 0$ when $c_1 x + c_2 t = \pi n$. Solving for the x, while ignoring trivial solutions:

$$ x = \frac{n \pi - c_2 t}{c_1} $$

The velocity of this wave is:

$$ \frac{dx}{dt} = -\frac{c_2}{c_1} $$

Similarly for $\psi_2$. At every integer $n \pi$ where $n=0,\pm 1, \pm 2, ...$, a sin function will be zero. Thus, $\psi_2 = 0$ when $c_1 x - c_2 t = \pi n$. Solving for x, for $\psi_2$:

$$ x = \frac{n \pi + c_2 t}{c_1} $$

The velocity of this wave is:

$$ \frac{dx}{dt} = \frac{c_2}{c_1} $$

The wavelength for each wave is twice the distance between two successive nodes. In other words,

$$ \lambda = 2(x_{n} - x_{n-1}) = \frac{2 \pi}{c_1} $$

Solution b

Find $\psi_+ = \psi_1 + \psi_2 \; \textrm{ and } \; \psi_- = \psi_1 - \psi_2$.

$$ \begin{aligned} \psi_+ &= \sin (c_1 x + c_2 t) + \sin (c_1 x - c_2 t) \\[4pt] &= \sin (c_1 x ) \cos (c_2 t) + \cancel{\cos(c_1 x) \sin(c_1 t)} + \sin (c_1 x ) \cos (c_2 t) - \cancel{\cos(c_1 x) \sin(c_1 t)} \\[4pt] &= 2\sin (c_1 x ) \cos (c_2 t) \end{aligned} $$

This should have a node at every $x= n \pi / c_1$ and

$$ \begin{aligned} \psi_- &= \sin (c_1 x + c_2 t) - \sin (c_1 x - c_2 t) \\[4pt] &= \cancel{\sin (c_1 x ) \cos (c_2 t)} + \cos(c_1 x) \sin(c_1 t) - \cancel{\sin (c_1 x ) \cos (c_2 t)} + \cos(c_1 x) \sin(c_1 t) \\[4pt] &= 2\cos (c_1 x ) \sin (c_2 t) \end{aligned} $$

exercises.prompt: Verify that Equation 2.4.3 is the general form for differential equations of the form of Equation 2.4.2.

answer.solution:
In order to show that

$$ X(x)=A e^{\sqrt{x} x}+B e^{-\sqrt{x} x} \tag{2.4.6} $$

is a general solution to the differential equation

$$ \frac{d^{2} X(x)}{d x^{2}}+p^{2} X(x)=0. $$

We then have to take the second derivative of Equation 2.4.6 and substitute it and the original function into the appropriate locations in Equation 2.4.3 and verify that it does in fact equal $0$.

First we have to take the first and then second derivative of Equation 2.4.6

$$ \begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{d x}\left(A e^{\sqrt{k x}}+B e^{-\sqrt{k} x}\right) &=\sqrt{k} A e^{\sqrt{k x}}-\sqrt{k} B e^{-\sqrt{k x}} \\[4pt] \dfrac{d^{2}}{d x^{2}}\left(A e^{\sqrt{k x}}+B e^{-\sqrt{k} x}\right) &=k A e^{\sqrt{k x}}+k B e^{-\sqrt{k x}} \end{aligned} $$

Now that we have the second derivative of Equation 2.4.6 we plug the relevant values into Equation 2.4.2

$$ \begin{aligned} \dfrac{d^{2} X(x)}{d x^{2}}+p^{2} X(x)=0 \\ k A e^{\sqrt{k} x}+k B e^{-\sqrt{k} x}+p^{2}\left(A e^{\sqrt{k} x}+B e^{-\sqrt{k} x}\right) \overset{?}{=} 0 \end{aligned} $$

We are given in Equation 2.4.2 that

$$ k=-p^{2} $$

So

$$ p^{2}=-k $$

Now we can plug that into our differential equation to simplify

$$ \begin{aligned} k A e^{\sqrt{k} x}+k B e^{-\sqrt{k} x} - k\left(A e^{\sqrt{k} x}+B e^{-\sqrt{k} x} \right) &\overset{?}{=} 0 \\[4pt] \bcancel{ k A e^{\sqrt{k x}}} + \cancel{k B e^{-\sqrt{k x}}} - \bcancel{k A e^{\sqrt{k x}}} - \cancel{k B e^{-\sqrt{k x}}} & \overset{\checkmark}{=} 0 \end{aligned} $$

As all of these terms cancel to equal 0, we prove that the solution given is a general solution to the differential equation. It is important to remember though that it is not the only solution to the differential equation.

exercises.source_id: can be expanded to natural frequencies
exercises.prompt: A guitar string 0.65 m long is held fixed at both ends, and waves travel along it at 410 m/s. What are the natural frequencies of its first three normal modes?

answer.solution: Equation 2.4.16 gives $ u_n = nv/2L$. Here $2L = 1.30$ m, so $ u_1 = (410\ ext{m/s})/(1.30\ ext{m}) = 315.4$ Hz. The overtones are whole multiples of it: $ u_2 = 2 u_1 = 630.8$ Hz and $ u_3 = 3 u_1 = 946.2$ Hz.

exercises.source_id: the total solution can be expressed as a sum of all possible solutions
exercises.prompt:
A string 0.60 m long, held fixed at both ends, carries waves at 240 m/s. It is released from rest and moves as

$$ u(x,t) = G_1 \cos (\omega_1 t) \sin \left(\dfrac{\pi x}{L}\right) + G_3 \cos (\omega_3 t) \sin \left(\dfrac{3\pi x}{L}\right) $$

with $G_1$ and $G_3$ both nonzero.

  1. Where between the ends does the $n = 3$ mode have its nodes? Give the nearer one to $x = 0$ first.
  2. How long after its release is the string first back in its starting shape?

parts.hint: $\sin(3\pi x/L)$ is zero where $3x/L$ is a whole number.
Each mode must have finished a whole number of periods.

answer.solution:
a. The $n = 3$ mode is zero where $\sin(3\pi x/L) = 0$, that is at $x = L/3$ and $x = 2L/3$ between the ends: 0.20 m and 0.40 m.

b. The string is back in its starting shape when both $\cos(\omega_1 t)$ and $\cos(\omega_3 t)$ are back at 1. Since $\omega_3 = 3\omega_1$, the third mode returns three times for each return of the first, so the first time both are back is one period of the fundamental, $1/\nu_1 = 2L/v = (1.20\ \text{m})/(240\ \text{m/s}) = 5.0 \times 10^{-3}$ s, or 5.0 ms.

footnotes.html: The $\sqrt{K}$ terms meant are those of the general solution $X(x) = Ae^{\sqrt{K}x} + Be^{-\sqrt{K}x}$, Equation 2.4.3 on this page (Equation 2.2.9 in Section 2.2); Equation 2.4.5 is the solution in cosines and sines.
Equations 2.4.4a and 2.4.4b are the book's labels for the two separated equations of Section 2.2: the temporal one is Equation 2.2.7 and the spatial one Equation 2.2.8.
The ansatz is $u(x,t) = X(x)T(t)$, Equation 2.2.3; Equation 2.4.1 is $K = -p^2$.
$n\pi/L$ is the spatial constant $p$ of mode $n$. The mode's angular frequency is $\omega_n = n\pi v/L$.

In the second line of each sum the key prints $\sin(c_1 t)$ where $\sin(c_2 t)$ is meant. It also leaves out the nodes of $\psi_-$: $2\cos(c_1 x)\sin(c_2 t)$ is zero at every $x = (n + \tfrac{1}{2})\pi/c_1$.
The key prints $e^{\sqrt{x}x}$, and below both $e^{\sqrt{kx}}$ and $e^{\sqrt{k}x}$. The function meant throughout is $X(x) = Ae^{\sqrt{K}x} + Be^{-\sqrt{K}x}$, with $k$ standing for $K$.
The equation the function is substituted into is Equation 2.4.2, and $K = -p^2$, which the key later cites as Equation 2.4.2, is Equation 2.4.1.

then.why: Equation 2.2.19 solves $d^2y/dx^2 - k^2 y = 0$; the separated equation has that form with $k^2 = K$.

steps.cap: With $K = -p^2$, the square root is $\sqrt{K} = ip$.
For the second exponential take $\theta = -px$: cosine is even and sine is odd.

assumes.text: New complex constants $C = A + B$ and $D = i(A - B)$.
The string is held at zero at its left end: $X(0) = 0$.
The string is held at zero at its right end: $X(L) = 0$.
If $D = 0$ as well, $X(x) = 0$ everywhere: the trivial solution, which we ignore.
A sine is zero only at a whole multiple of $\pi$, and $n = 0$ is again the trivial solution, so $n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$
